title: After 1997, 175 south-east Australian catchments lost one fifth to one quarter of their runoff response to rain in three rain products; eastern US runoff had a constant offset instead
abstract: Question: why does runoff in south-east Australia (SE-AU) stay low after the Millennium Drought, also in wet years, while US catchments show no such state? Which part of the flow carries the deficit, and how did the rainfall-runoff relation change? Approach: 175 SE-AU catchments (CAMELS-AUS v2.03, 1951-2021), 260 eastern and 279 western US CAMELS catchments (USGS daily flow, 1951-2025), and SW Western Australia as a groundwater-decline control. We separated baseflow and quickflow with three methods and fitted annual flow on rain, previous-year rain and temperature for 1951-1996 only. We used AGCD, SILO and CRU TS rain in Australia, and nClimGrid and CRU in the US. Results: in 2010-2021, SE-AU baseflow and quickflow were 13.9% and 14.3% below the relation (difference +0.4 points, 95% CI -5.7 to +5.0). Thus the deficit is not specific to baseflow. Eastern US components also lost equal fractions (-5.5% and -6.8%). In a post hoc test, the SE-AU rain slope of runoff was 22-26% lower with all three rain products (19-26% with a quadratic term). These values were below all nine pre-1997 window-null values. The SE-AU deficit was 16% in wet years and 2% in dry years. The eastern US slope did not decrease (-0.3%); its deficit was an offset of -7%. AGCD rain increased by 2.3% relative to both SILO and CRU near 1997, and SILO and CRU agreed. The SE-AU offset at mean rain was -14.5% with AGCD, -7.5% with SILO and -1.4% with CRU. Conclusion: the SE-AU change is a loss of runoff sensitivity to rain that is largest in wet years, not a baseflow loss or a constant offset. Limitations: slope and rain-step tests are post hoc; SE-AU already drifted in 1981-1996; annual linear models; the correct rain product is unknown; causes were not tested.

display.caption: Runoff residual against the annual rain anomaly in 1951-1996 (fit years) and in 2010 to end of record. After 2010 the south-east Australian deficit grows with rain; the eastern US deficit is about constant.
Change of the rain slope and offset at mean rain in 2010 to end of record, for three rain products, with 95% intervals and the range of nine pre-1997 window-null tests.
Ratios of annual rain products relative to 1960-1996. AGCD increases by about 2% near 1997 relative to SILO and CRU; SILO and CRU agree.

citations.reason: We explain why the low-runoff state persisted through wet years: the deficit is largest in wet years.
Seasonal rain terms did not remove the deficit; we test the flow components and the rain slope.
We use its basin nClimGrid water-year climate table and its NWIS retrieval code; our annual runoff totals agree with its table.
US hidden low-runoff states occurred at the stationary rate; we show the eastern US change is an offset, not a slope loss.
US groundwater did not stay low; our component partition finds no baseflow-specific deficit.
Global GRACE storage did not stay low after droughts.
It found eastern US and SE-AU shifts of similar size in SD units; we show they differ in form and that part of the SE-AU level deficit depends on an AGCD rain step.
It found that wet years did not reduce the SE-AU deficit; we quantify the slope loss with three rain products.
